planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring once frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; amla needs a long frost-free season and full sun to fruit well. Grafted cultivars fruit years sooner than seedlings and preserve known fruit quality; seedling trees vary widely in fruit size, sourness, and precocity.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; amla is a deciduous small tree native to South and Southeast Asia, grown for its round, pale green, translucent fruits that are extremely high in vitamin C and intensely sour and astringent when fresh. The tree tolerates poor, rocky soils and considerable drought once established, and produces feathery, fine-textured foliage that drops in the dry season. Fruits ripen in fall to early winter and are typically pickled, candied, dried, or processed into juice, chutney, and the Ayurvedic preserve chyawanprash rather than eaten out of hand. Trees are usually grafted onto seedling rootstock for faster, more reliable bearing and are sensitive to hard freezes, restricting outdoor culture to the warmest parts of zones 9-11 or container growing elsewhere.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Emblica (Indian Gooseberry)
California Rare Fruit Growers — Amla Fruit Facts
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products — Emblic

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root grafted trees in early spring while dormant; Pioneer was selected for larger, sweeter fruit than the wild species and benefits from a second cornelian cherry cultivar nearby for heavier fruit set, though it will set some fruit alone.

directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; Pioneer is a fruit-selected cultivar of Cornus mas, a small multi-stemmed tree that opens clusters of tiny yellow flowers on bare branches in very early spring, weeks before forsythia. Its oblong, cherry-red fruits ripen in midsummer and drop as they soften, so most growers harvest by shaking the tree onto a tarp or gathering fallen fruit daily; the tart, plum-like flesh is used for syrup, jam, liqueur, and traditional Eastern European preserves. The tree is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerates urban conditions and a range of soils, and is largely untroubled by pests or diseases that plague other stone fruit. Pioneer bears earlier and more heavily than unselected seedlings, typically fruiting within three to four years of planting.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Cornelian Cherry Dogwood
Morton Arboretum — Cornus mas
One Green World Nursery — Cornelian Cherry Cultivars

planting.note: Plant grafted, bare-root or container trees in early spring or fall while dormant; Breda Giant is self-fertile and needs no pollinator. Choose a sheltered, sunny site, as the large white spring flowers can be damaged by hard late frosts.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Breda Giant is a classic Dutch medlar selection prized for producing unusually large, russeted brown fruit on a small, gnarled, ornamental tree with showy white spring flowers and good fall color. Fruit is rock-hard and inedible at harvest in late fall and must be 'bletted' — stored in a cool place for several weeks after the first frosts until it softens and browns internally to a soft, spiced, wine-like custard texture before eating fresh or making jelly and butter. The tree is very cold-hardy, tolerates poor soils, and is largely pest- and disease-free, making it an easy, low-maintenance addition to a home orchard once its unusual harvest-and-ripen routine is understood.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Mespilus germanica (Medlar)
Raintree Nursery — Medlar Varieties
Chris Bowers & Sons (UK) — Breda Giant Medlar

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring against a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade; Eastern Prince is a self-fertile, perfect-flowered selection so a single plant will set fruit, unlike most schisandra which are dioecious and need separate male and female vines.

directions: Plant in partial shade with morning sun in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Eastern Prince is a self-fertile cultivar of Schisandra chinensis, the 'five-flavor berry' used for centuries in Chinese and Russian herbal medicine and prized in its native forests for fruit and foliage said to combine sour, sweet, salty, bitter, and pungent notes in one berry. The twining vine bears small, waxy white flowers in spring followed by long, pendant clusters of glossy red berries in late summer, best used for juice, tinctures, syrup, and jam rather than fresh eating due to their intense tartness. Because it is perfect-flowered rather than dioecious, Eastern Prince fruits reliably without a separate pollinator vine, making it far more practical for small gardens than seed-grown schisandra. Provide sturdy support and consistent moisture, and mulch to keep roots cool.
sources: One Green World Nursery — Schisandra Eastern Prince
Cornell Small Farms Program — Schisandra chinensis Production Guide
Raintree Nursery — Schisandra Varieties

planting.note: Fall-sow stratified seed outdoors, or plant bare-root or container nursery stock in early spring; Sierra plum is largely self-incompatible, so plant two or more seedlings or a second Prunus subcordata clone nearby to ensure good fruit set.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Sierra plum is a thicket-forming small tree or large shrub native to the mountains of California and southern Oregon, valued by home orchardists and native plant gardeners for its drought tolerance, fragrant white spring flowers, and small, tart-sweet red-to-purple plums that ripen in late summer. Fruit quality is variable from seed, so growers who want reliable, larger fruit often select and propagate superior wild clones by cuttings or grafting. The species is tough and adaptable to rocky, thin mountain soils and needs little supplemental water once established, but it suckers readily and can form dense thickets if not managed. Fruit is traditionally used fresh, for jam and jelly, and was an important food source for indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest and California.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Klamath Plum (Prunus subcordata)
Calscape (California Native Plant Society) — Prunus subcordata
Las Pilitas Nursery — Prunus subcordata

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring against a sturdy arbor, fence, or pergola in full sun; California wild grape tolerates heat, drought, and periodic flooding once established and needs little irrigation after the first two seasons.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil along a strong support; California wild grape is a vigorous, deciduous native vine of streambanks and canyons from Oregon to Baja California, grown both as a fast-growing ornamental shade vine and for its small, tart, blue-black grapes that ripen in early fall. Fruit is seedy and sharply acidic, used mainly for jelly, juice, and wine rather than fresh eating, and is an important wildlife food. The species is a parent of the widely planted, purple-leaved ornamental cultivars 'Roger's Red' and 'Rogers Red', and its rootstock has been used in grape breeding for drought and Pierce's disease tolerance. Once established, the deep-rooted vine is remarkably drought-tolerant and requires only annual dormant-season pruning to control its vigorous growth.
sources: Calscape (California Native Plant Society) — Vitis californica
UC Davis Department of Viticulture and Enology — Native California Grapes
Las Pilitas Nursery — Vitis californica

common_name: California Black Walnut (Southern California Black Walnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container seedlings in late winter to early spring; site well away from vegetable gardens and sensitive ornamentals, since like other walnuts it produces root-zone juglone that is toxic to many plants.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; California black walnut is a multi-trunked, drought-adapted tree native to the coastal ranges and foothills of Southern and Central California, historically an important food source for indigenous peoples and still valued by native plant and wildlife gardeners for its small, thick-shelled, richly flavored nuts. It is far more heat- and drought-tolerant than eastern black walnut and has long been used as rootstock for grafting English walnut in California orchards because of its vigor and disease resistance. Trees are slow-growing and produce nuts within a juglone-rich root zone, so keep sensitive plants at a distance. Given its wild, spreading habit and long lifespan, it suits large properties, hedgerows, and wildlife plantings more than small home gardens.
sources: Calscape (California Native Plant Society) — Juglans californica
USDA Forest Service Silvics Manual — Juglans californica
UC Agriculture and Natural Resources — California Walnut Species
